failure_classes.assumptions: A clean-ish process kill (SIGKILL/abort): only the process's own buffers are lost; every byte that completed a write syscall survives in the OS page cache. The strongest class (tests/crash_recovery.rs).
failure_classes.name: process

failure_classes.assumptions: A kernel panic/reboot: userspace buffers and the OS page cache are lost; bytes the device already accepted survive because the device write-back cache is not lost; writes may be reordered.
failure_classes.name: kernel

failure_classes.assumptions: An un-clean storage power loss: only flushed bytes survive, and per the flush/durable-loss profile writes may be reordered, partially applied, or torn (src/powerloss.rs, Phases 17/23).
failure_classes.name: storage

model_assumptions: This is a deterministic, in-process simulated device (src/powerloss.rs), not hardware. A green run shows recovery correct relative to the model's assumed device semantics; it does not prove real-hardware durability.

The distinguished failure classes differ only in which volatile layer is lost, and therefore in how many un-flushed bytes are retained: Process (page cache) >= Kernel (device cache) >= Storage (nothing).

For OrFS, Process and Kernel retain the same bytes: the commit path has no acknowledged-but-unwritten userspace data, so the two coincide for the acknowledged contract; they differ only in that Kernel may reorder the retained writes.
An in-flight completion (a sync that never completed) surfaces as OrfsError::InFlight (EAGAIN): transient, non-latching, never durable.
Metadata tearing targets the watermark, a directory entry, and an interior framing sector of a committed segment -- not only a file's trailing sector.
The generation manifest / catalogue lives outside the log directory and is therefore not modelled by the log-directory device; it is covered by the manifestation courts (Phases 42/78).

per_mode_contract.may_be_lost_before_the_point: ordered-but-unsynced mutations may be lost under Storage; they survive under Process/Kernel
mutations within the current batch may be lost under Storage

precedence: retained(process) superset retained(kernel) superset retained(storage); the acknowledged-durability contract holds for every class while the unacknowledged tail differs

residual_property.detectable: a commit watermark ahead of the surviving committed bytes (a lost/truncated trailing committed segment) is DETECTED: the open is refused, never silently shortened
residual_property.reason: The watermark is written AFTER the bytes it describes and is never allowed to rewrite committed history (non-withdrawal). Detecting the loss of those not-yet-watermarked bytes would require an additional synchronous metadata write on the acknowledgment path (changing the durability contract and cost) or rewriting committed bytes (forbidden). The gap is inherent to any scheme that cannot rewrite committed history, so it is recorded as an explicit property rather than claimed closed.
residual_property.undetectable: the loss of durable bytes between the last persisted watermark and the committed root is UNDETECTED by the watermark alone (the documented residual window; docs/LIMITATIONS.md 6, docs/RECOVERY.md 5)
